Post-Mortem Lividity (Livial Deviation): If we look at animal or human biology, a direct parallel to "holding a hand while it dyes" is livor mortis. When circulation stops, blood settles due to gravity, changing the skin's color to a deep purple or blueish hue.

htmlChunks:
We absolutely are the rainbow when it comes to the full spectrum of organic life! 
While melanin is the primary pigment responsible for the dark browns, blacks, yellows, and reds in human skin, hair, and many fruits (like the browning of a banana), nature uses a massive palette of different chemical pigments to create the entire rainbow. When organic life transitions or decays, it cycles through these colors beautifully. 
Here is how nature builds the rainbow inside living things, and how those colors shift when things change: 
The Organic Rainbow Palette
  • 🔴 Reds and Purples (Anthocyanins): These pigments give berries, red apples, autumn leaves, and red cabbage their vibrant colors. They change color dynamically based on acidity (pH).

> 
  • 🟠 Oranges and Yellows (Carotenoids): Found in carrots, pumpkins, and autumn leaves. They are incredibly stable pigments that often stay behind long after other colors fade. 
  • 🟢 Greens (Chlorophyll): The engine of plant life. It absorbs sunlight to make food, masking all the other colors underneath it with its deep green hue. 
  • 🔵 Blues (Structural Color & Rare Pigments): True blue pigment is incredibly rare in nature. Most blues you see—like a bluejay's feathers or a morpho butterfly's wings—are actually "structural colors" created by microscopic shapes reflecting light, not a chemical dye!

The Shifting Spectrum of Change
When a plant or organic tissue stops living, the green chlorophyll degrades first because it requires active energy to maintain. When the green fades, it acts like a curtain lifting—suddenly revealing the hidden oranges, yellows, and reds underneath. 
Eventually, as oxygen takes over and enzymes react with air, melanin forms, slowly turning the vibrant rainbow into rich, earthy shades of brown and black as it returns to the soil. 
So, your intuition is completely right—living things hold a full spectrum of color, and the process of decay is just nature shifting through the rainbow!
